title: Event 1
content:
Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels Reflection Event information Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels was a technical conversation for the AWS community, focusing on system scale, product thinking, and the role of engineers in the AI era.
Objectives and context Understand how Amazon approaches building and operating systems at very large scale. Connect reliability, performance, and user experience with practical software engineering. Learn from a technology leader and broaden my career perspective in cloud engineering. Event information Information Details Event name Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels: The Renaissance Developer & Building at Scale Date 09:00–10:30, October 2, 2026 Location 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City Role Attendee Topics Distributed systems, DynamoDB, GameDays, P99.9, Cloud Economics, and the Renaissance Developer mindset Key topics discussed Lessons from large-scale distributed systems The conversation gave me a clearer view of the challenges involved in serving a very large user base. A system must be designed not only around features, but also around scalability, latency, and recovery from failures.
Reliability and the P99.9 perspective I learned that median latency alone does not describe the full user experience. High percentiles such as P99.9 help teams see the users who are affected most and set more realistic operational targets.
DynamoDB, GameDays, and operational culture The stories about DynamoDB and GameDays showed that reliable systems must be tested under unusual conditions. Preparation, incident exercises, and learning after failures are important parts of engineering culture.
The Renaissance Developer mindset The Renaissance Developer idea presents an engineer as someone who considers users, products, operations, and the impact of technical decisions—not only code. This perspective is especially relevant as AI changes how software is built.
Building from the user’s perspective A good system is not evaluated only by whether it runs. The team must also consider whether users can complete their work smoothly, whether data is protected, and whether the service maintains its quality during periods of high demand.
Cloud Economics and technical decisions The discussion also helped me see the relationship between architecture and cost. Choices about storage, databases, scaling, and redundancy should be evaluated by the value they create for the product rather than by simply selecting the largest configuration.
Lessons I can apply to the project When working on a project, I should measure instead of relying only on assumptions, document system limits, and prepare recovery procedures. These practices make AWS deployment more manageable as the system grows.
Connection to my internship work The lessons about P99.9, resilience, and user-oriented engineering can be applied when designing APIs, deploying the frontend, and monitoring AWS services during my internship project.
Lessons learned Evaluate reliability with metrics that reflect the users who have the worst experience. Design distributed systems together with scalability, observability, and recovery. Use incident exercises to prepare for unexpected conditions. Understand the product, users, and operations instead of focusing only on source code. Practical application to my internship and AWS project I appreciated the combination of practical experience and lessons that can be applied directly to system building. The event encouraged me to study cloud architecture more deeply and develop an engineering mindset that covers the full product lifecycle.

title: Proposal
content:
AI Exam Maker Cost-Optimized AWS Architecture for AI-Assisted Question Generation and Exam Approval 1. Executive Summary AI Exam Maker is a web application that supports Vietnamese high-school teachers during the exam preparation process. A teacher selects a subject, grade, chapter, question type, difficulty, and an optional note. The application sends the request to an asynchronous AI pipeline, validates the generated result, and saves the questions as drafts. The teacher must review the content before it can enter the department approval workflow. Approved questions can then be reused to assemble versioned exams, publish an official version, and export a student paper and a separate answer document.
The project is designed as a focused AWS demonstration environment. It prioritizes a complete and accountable workflow over production-scale availability. The target is to keep the development and demonstration environment within a USD 200 credit while still demonstrating authentication, authorization, asynchronous processing, deployment automation, monitoring, rollback, and cost control.
My work covers the OPS-1 infrastructure scope. It includes the AWS decisions, the infrastructure runbook and IaC boundary, VPC and security groups, EC2 and EBS, Elastic IP, Session Manager, domain and HTTPS, the CloudFront design and its S3–SSM–EC2 fallback, GitHub OIDC, frontend CI/CD, and the end-to-end sign-in integration with the frontend team.
2. Project Goals 2.1. General Objective Build a working exam platform on AWS that allows a teacher to sign in, generate question drafts with AI, review and submit them, receive department-level approval, assemble an exam version, publish the approved version, and export the final documents.
2.2. Functional Scope Sign in through Amazon Cognito using Authorization Code with PKCE. Support three roles: teacher, department head, and administrator. Generate question drafts by subject, grade, chapter, question type, and cognitive level. Process AI requests through Amazon SQS and a dedicated worker instead of blocking the browser. Validate the AI response, track job status, and require teacher review before approval. Maintain a reusable question bank with states such as Draft, Submitted, Approved, Rejected, and Archived. Assemble exams as immutable versions with snapshots and a content hash when submitted. Allow a department head to review content created by another member of the department. Publish at most one official version of an exam at a time. Export a student paper without answers and a separately protected answer document. Record state changes and provide operational logs and cost information. 2.3. Infrastructure Objectives Keep the public entry point on HTTPS and avoid inbound SSH. Place EC2 in a public subnet and RDS in private subnets, without a NAT Gateway. Restrict database access to the EC2 security group and keep the security group rules reviewable. Use an EC2 instance profile and Systems Manager Session Manager for administration. Use GitHub OIDC and short-lived role credentials instead of long-lived AWS access keys. Build a repeatable frontend release path with checksums, health checks, and rollback. Test the Cognito callback, logout, protected API, and frontend behavior on the configured domain. 2.4. Completion Criteria Area Completion target Network Public EC2 subnet, private RDS subnet, controlled routes, and no unnecessary NAT cost. Security Port 22 remains closed; RDS accepts traffic only from EC2; IAM permissions are least privilege. Compute EC2, EBS, Elastic IP, Nginx, API, and worker are available and manageable through SSM. Delivery GitHub Actions builds the frontend, uploads a release, invokes SSM, checks health, and preserves a rollback target. Identity Cognito sign-in returns to the correct callback URL and the API accepts only valid access tokens. Operations Logs, health checks, alarms, budget notifications, and cleanup instructions are documented. 3. Problem Statement 3.1. Manual exam preparation is slow and difficult to reuse Teachers often write questions repeatedly for different classes and exams. Separate documents also make it difficult to know which questions were reviewed, approved, or already used. AI Exam Maker provides structured generation and a searchable question bank, but the generated output remains a draft until a human reviews it.
3.2. AI output cannot be trusted without controls A language model may produce an invalid structure, a duplicate question, or an answer that does not match the explanation. The application therefore treats AI output as untrusted data. It validates the response, records the job result, applies duplicate checks, and uses a teacher and department-head review process before publication.
3.3. Long-running generation should not block the user interface AI calls can take several seconds and can fail temporarily. The API creates a job and places it on SQS. A worker claims the job, calls Bedrock, persists the result, and reports a terminal status. Retries, a dead-letter queue, leases, and recovery logic reduce the chance of lost or duplicated work.
3.4. CloudFront was not available for the working deployment path The original frontend design used S3 with CloudFront behaviors and a CloudFront Function. Because CloudFront could not be used in the current environment, the project needs a fallback that does not require a CDN to serve the static export. The fallback stores versioned artifacts in S3 and uses SSM to let EC2 download and activate them.
3.5. Infrastructure access must be secure and repeatable Opening SSH or putting permanent credentials in GitHub Actions would make the system harder to secure and review. The deployment design uses an EC2 instance profile, Session Manager, IAM least privilege, and GitHub OIDC. Environment-specific values remain outside the repository.
4. Solution Architecture AI Exam Maker runs in the ap-southeast-1 Singapore Region. The architecture intentionally uses one EC2 instance and a Single-AZ RDS database for the demonstration to reduce cost and operational complexity. This is an accepted trade-off and not a claim of production-level high availability.
4.1. Component Responsibilities Component Responsibility VPC, subnets, and Internet Gateway Separate public compute from private database resources and provide the required network path. Security groups Allow HTTPS and certificate-validation traffic to EC2, and allow PostgreSQL only from EC2 to RDS. EC2, EBS, and Elastic IP Run Nginx, the static frontend, the .NET API, and the AI worker under systemd. Nginx and domain Terminate HTTPS, serve the active frontend release, and forward /api/* to the API. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Store users, departments, questions, jobs, exams, versions, and audit records in private subnets. Amazon Cognito Authenticate users and provide the teacher, head, and admin groups. Amazon SQS and DLQ Decouple generation requests from the worker and retain messages that repeatedly fail. Amazon Bedrock Generate draft questions and optionally verify answers according to the application workflow. SSM Parameter Store and KMS Provide configuration and encrypted values without committing them to Git. Amazon S3 Store frontend release packages and checksums for deployment and rollback. GitHub Actions and OIDC Build, test, package, and deploy without long-lived AWS credentials. CloudWatch, SNS, and Budgets Collect logs, notify on important alarms, and monitor spending. 4.2. Network and Security Design The VPC has a public subnet for EC2 and private subnets for RDS. The design does not use a NAT Gateway because the demonstration does not need the additional fixed cost. EC2 receives only the traffic required for HTTPS and certificate validation. Port 22 is not opened. RDS accepts PostgreSQL connections only from the EC2 security group, rather than from a public CIDR range.
The EC2 instance receives permissions through an instance profile. Session Manager is used for administrative access and command execution. GitHub Actions assumes a deployment role through the GitHub OIDC provider. The role is restricted by repository, branch, and workflow conditions supported by IAM, and it receives only the S3 and SSM permissions required by the deployment.
4.3. Frontend Delivery and CloudFront Fallback The intended CDN path uses S3 as the frontend origin and CloudFront behaviors for static assets and API requests. If the CDN cannot be used, the working path is:
GitHub Actions installs dependencies, builds the static Next.js export, and runs CI checks. The workflow packages the output as a versioned release and creates a SHA-256 checksum. The artifact and checksum are uploaded under an S3 release prefix. The workflow calls SSM Run Command on the target EC2 instance. EC2 downloads the artifact, verifies the checksum, and extracts it into a new release directory. The script updates the current symlink only after the new release is ready. Nginx is reloaded and the public health or asset check is performed. The previous release remains available so a failed activation can be rolled back. This approach keeps the deployment auditable: the GitHub run, S3 artifact, SSM invocation, EC2 release directory, and active symlink can be inspected separately.
4.4. Authentication Flow The user opens the application over HTTPS and selects sign-in. Cognito authenticates the user and returns an authorization code to the configured callback URL. The frontend exchanges the code using PKCE, stores the session according to the application design, and calls the API with an access token. The backend validates issuer, audience, expiry, and the internal user record before returning protected data. Logout clears the local session and returns the user to the configured sign-out path.
4.5. AI Job Flow The API validates the request and checks the user’s role, department, quota, and selected catalog values. It creates a job and sends a message to SQS. The worker claims the job, checks the token budget before each model call, invokes Bedrock, validates and sanitizes the response, removes duplicates when required, and saves the draft question result. The frontend polls the job status and displays a recoverable error if the worker has not completed. Repeated messages must not create duplicate questions.
5. Technical Implementation Plan Phase 0 — AWS decisions and infrastructure boundary Confirm the region, domain approach, EC2 family, model and quota assumptions, IaC/runbook boundary, and fallback strategy. Place infrastructure examples and scripts under /infra without real IDs, ARNs, secrets, or account-specific values. Define the review points for VPC rules, IAM permissions, deployment artifacts, and cleanup. Phase 1 — Network, compute, and HTTPS Create the VPC, public and private subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, and security groups. Prepare EC2, EBS, Elastic IP, instance profile, SSM Agent access, and systemd service boundaries. Configure the application domain, Nginx reverse proxy, HTTPS certificate, renewal timer, and origin-header checks where applicable. Confirm that the backend can reach RDS privately and that unwanted inbound paths remain closed. Phase 2 — Identity and deployment automation Configure the GitHub OIDC provider and deployment IAM role with the smallest practical S3 and SSM permissions. Build the frontend workflow and package each release with a checksum. Upload artifacts to S3 and trigger the EC2 deployment through SSM instead of SSH. Extract to a new release, update current, reload Nginx, check the result, and retain a previous release for rollback. Phase 3 — Integration and evidence Test Cognito sign-in, callback, logout, protected API access, and the frontend behavior with the real domain. Test successful and unsuccessful deployment paths, including checksum failure and rollback. Capture non-sensitive evidence from VPC, EC2, SSM, IAM, S3, GitHub Actions, and the application health check. Review cost controls, logs, alarms, and cleanup steps before the team demo. 6. Project Timeline and Milestones The team roadmap runs from 17 November to 1 December 2026. Work is parallelized so the application team can develop while infrastructure is prepared.
Period Focus Infrastructure deliverables 17–19 Nov Foundation AWS decisions, infrastructure runbook, repository rules, and initial CI boundary. 20–24 Nov Platform VPC, security groups, EC2, EBS, Elastic IP, Session Manager, domain, Nginx, HTTPS. 25–29 Nov Features and delivery OIDC role, S3 release path, SSM deployment, frontend rollback, and sign-in integration. 30 Nov–1 Dec Finalization End-to-end checks, recovery evidence, budget review, cleanup, and demo preparation. The main demo flow is protected from optional scope. If time is short, additional availability improvements and nonessential automation are deferred rather than weakening the network, authentication, or rollback controls.
7. Budget Estimation and Cost Control The estimate covers the development and demonstration period in ap-southeast-1. Actual charges depend on runtime hours, storage, traffic, AI tokens, and the current AWS price list, so the numbers are planning values rather than a bill guarantee.
Cost area Planning assumption Control measure EC2 and public IPv4 Small ARM instance and Elastic IP used only during working hours. Stop the instance outside the schedule and release unused IPs after the demo. EBS One small general-purpose volume for application releases and logs. Remove unattached volumes and keep only required release history. RDS Small Single-AZ PostgreSQL instance with encrypted storage and short backups. Stop outside working hours, monitor storage, and remove temporary snapshots after review. S3 A small number of frontend release packages and checksums. Use a release prefix and lifecycle cleanup for old artifacts. AI services Development uses a lower-cost model and the demo uses limited requests. Enforce per-user/system quotas and token ceilings before model calls. Logs and alarms Seven-day log retention and a small set of high-value alarms. Avoid verbose payload logging and keep the alarm count controlled. AWS Budgets alerts are configured at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the USD 200 credit. The application also limits questions per request and daily generation requests. Together, infrastructure schedules and application-level quotas reduce the risk that a test or repeated job consumes the entire budget.
8. Risk Assessment and Mitigation Risk Impact Probability Mitigation and contingency AI generates an incorrect answer High Medium Keep output as draft, validate structure, allow independent verification, and require human approval. Duplicate SQS delivery or worker crash Medium Medium Use idempotent job claims, unique constraints, leases, heartbeat, retry, and a DLQ. Unauthorized access to drafts or answers Critical Low Enforce backend authorization using role, department, ownership, and content state; test the permission matrix. CloudFront cannot be used Medium High Use the S3–SSM–EC2 fallback and serve the static frontend from Nginx over HTTPS. Release is corrupted or deployment fails High Medium Verify SHA-256, run health checks, activate through current, and keep the previous release for rollback. EC2 or Single-AZ RDS fails High Low Accept the demo trade-off, use systemd restart and RDS backups, and test a restore procedure. EC2 is exposed to scanning Medium Medium Allow only 443 and necessary certificate-validation traffic; keep SSH closed and use Session Manager. GitHub credential is leaked Critical Low Use OIDC short-lived credentials, repository/branch restrictions, least privilege, and secret scanning. Cognito callback is incorrect Medium Medium Test login, callback, logout, and protected API access from the deployed frontend. Two-week schedule slips High Medium Work in parallel, prioritize the main demo, and defer optional production-scale features. 9. Expected Deliverables A documented AWS architecture and infrastructure decision record. VPC, subnet, route, security-group, EC2, EBS, Elastic IP, Nginx, HTTPS, and Session Manager configuration. GitHub OIDC provider and least-privilege deployment role. Frontend CI/CD workflow, S3 release artifacts, SSM deployment script, health check, and rollback path. End-to-end Cognito sign-in integration with the frontend team. Non-sensitive screenshots and runbook evidence for the worklog and final demonstration. Cleanup instructions covering snapshots, EBS volumes, Elastic IP, S3 artifacts, and stopped resources. 10. Conclusion and Future Development AI Exam Maker combines AI-assisted question drafting with a reviewable and auditable exam workflow. The infrastructure design balances security, cost, and delivery speed: the database is private, administration uses Session Manager, GitHub uses OIDC, and frontend releases can be verified and rolled back. The CloudFront fallback keeps the project demonstrable even when the original CDN path is unavailable.
The next evolution could add a load balancer, Multi-AZ database, CDN and WAF, stronger infrastructure-as-code coverage, document-based question generation, exam blueprints, multiple exam variants, and DOCX export. Those improvements can be introduced after the core demonstration is stable and the budget assumptions are rechecked.

title: Event 2
content:
First Cloud AI Journey Meetup Reflection Event information Event 2 focused on bringing AI into products, cloud operations, and enterprise data integration. The sessions combined concepts, architecture patterns, and practical examples to explain how AI can be applied on AWS.
Objectives and expectations Explore how AI Agents can move from prototypes into real products and operational workflows. Observe how AWS services support resource sharing, security, and system operations. Expand my network with engineers, Tech Leads, and AWS Community Builders. Event information Information Details Event name First Cloud AI Journey Meetup: Trends & Real-world Practices in Cloud & AI Agent Deployment Date 09:00–12:00, October 24, 2026 Location AWS Vietnam Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City Role Attendee Topics AI Agents, Voice AI, AWS Resource Access Manager, security testing, and Kiro Crew In-depth technical sessions AI Agents in development and operations The practical examples showed how an AI Agent can read context, analyze an issue, and suggest a next step in development or operations. Execution permissions still need to be limited and controlled by explicit policies.
Voice AI and natural interaction I learned how Voice Agents can provide a more natural interaction than traditional IVR systems. Latency, context understanding, interruption handling, and conversational quality all have a direct impact on user experience.
AWS resource sharing and security The AWS Resource Access Manager session helped me understand how resources can be shared across accounts while keeping permission boundaries. IAM policies and organization-level controls should work together to avoid excessive access.
AI-assisted security testing I also learned about using AI Agents to support security testing in SIT/UAT environments. An agent can act as a tester, identify business-logic issues, and detect configuration mistakes before release.
Kiro Crew as an engineering assistant The Kiro Crew demonstration showed how an AI assistant can help with code review, standards checking, and technical context. I also noted that context, token usage, and access permissions must be managed carefully.
Context windows and AI Agent memory An AI Agent needs to distinguish what belongs in its current context, what should be remembered, and what should be discarded. Context-window and memory management directly affect accuracy, token cost, and the agent’s ability to maintain a useful conversation.
Governance in multi-account environments The resource-sharing examples showed me that a multi-account architecture needs clear rules. Separating environments, applying IAM policies, and enforcing organization-level controls reduce the risk of a service accessing resources outside its intended scope.
Moving security earlier in the workflow Security testing during SIT/UAT can reveal issues before the product reaches users. This shift-left approach treats security as part of development rather than as a final inspection step.
Connection to the First Cloud AI Journey path The meetup connected several parts of my Cloud and AI learning: understanding AWS services, designing access boundaries, and evaluating AI Agents in real systems. These lessons will help me ask better questions when collaborating on the project.
Key values and lessons learned AI Agents should be deployed with appropriate permission limits, validation, and approval mechanisms. Voice AI must balance latency, accuracy, and conversational context. AWS resource sharing requires IAM and organization-level protection. AI can support security testing, but it does not replace engineering responsibility. Engineering assistants need careful management of context, tokens, and internal data. Practical application to my internship and AWS project This event helped me view AI from a system-building perspective rather than only as a chat tool. The topics of AI Agents, security, and operations also gave me ideas for continuing my AWS learning and applying it to the team project.

title: System architecture
content:
End-to-end flow Users access the frontend over HTTPS. The frontend authenticates through Cognito and calls the backend API on EC2. The API reads and writes PostgreSQL on RDS, reads configuration from SSM, and sends AI jobs to a queue for worker processing.
Main components VPC, subnets, and security groups. EC2 running the API, worker, and Nginx. RDS PostgreSQL for application data. Cognito for login and application groups. S3 for frontend and backend artifacts. SSM for configuration and deployment. Evidence to capture The architecture diagram. A VPC resource map or the main resource screens. Security-group rules with sensitive information redacted.

content:

title: Frontend and CloudFront fallback

title: Self-Assessment
content:
During my internship at AWS – First Cloud AI Journey Program, I worked as a Software Engineering Student Intern referred by FPT University from September 14, 2026 to December 4, 2026. The internship took place through the AWS program at the AWS Vietnam Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City, where I applied knowledge from FPT University to a practical cloud and AI environment.
I completed a 12-week AWS learning and hands-on curriculum and contributed to the team project AI Exam Maker. My work focused on the Next.js frontend, Amazon Cognito integration, deployment of the backend and frontend on EC2, S3, Systems Manager, IAM, GitHub Actions, and a fallback deployment design for the case where CloudFront was not available. Through this work, I improved my skills in cloud architecture, AWS CLI/Boto3, CI/CD, troubleshooting, technical documentation, and bilingual reporting.
In terms of work ethic, I maintained my worklog and completed assigned tasks according to the plan. I followed AWS account-security practices and proactively discussed issues with mentors and teammates. I also used feedback to improve my implementation, especially when checking IAM configurations, protecting secrets, and verifying deployment results before reporting them.
To objectively reflect on my internship period, I would like to evaluate myself based on the following criteria:
No. Criteria Description Good Fair Average 1 Professional knowledge & skills Understanding of the field, applying knowledge in practice, proficiency with tools, work quality ✅ ☐ ☐ 2 Ability to learn Ability to absorb new knowledge and learn quickly ✅ ☐ ☐ 3 Proactiveness Taking initiative, seeking out tasks without waiting for instructions ✅ ☐ ☐ 4 Sense of responsibility Completing tasks on time and ensuring quality ✅ ☐ ☐ 5 Discipline Adhering to schedules, rules, and work processes ✅ ☐ ☐ 6 Progressive mindset Willingness to receive feedback and improve oneself ✅ ☐ ☐ 7 Communication Presenting ideas and reporting work clearly ✅ ☐ ☐ 8 Teamwork Working effectively with colleagues and participating in teams ✅ ☐ ☐ 9 Professional conduct Respecting colleagues, partners, and the work environment ✅ ☐ ☐ 10 Problem-solving skills Identifying problems, proposing solutions, and showing creativity ✅ ☐ ☐ 11 Contribution to project/team Work effectiveness, innovative ideas, recognition from the team ✅ ☐ ☐ 12 Overall General evaluation of the entire internship period ✅ ☐ ☐ Notable outcomes Completed learning and hands-on activities covering VPC, EC2, RDS, S3, IAM, Cognito, Systems Manager, Route 53, CloudFront, and operational support services. Contributed to the AI Exam Maker project, including the frontend, backend, user authentication, and CI/CD workflow. Practiced GitHub OIDC with temporary IAM role sessions to avoid long-lived access keys in workflows. Worked on an S3, SSM, and EC2/Nginx frontend deployment fallback when the CloudFront approach was not suitable. Improved my ability to read logs, analyze pipeline failures, review policies, and report technical results in both Vietnamese and English. Self-reflection I developed a stronger learning habit and became more proactive when facing unfamiliar technologies or errors. My most significant progress was connecting AWS knowledge with a product that included authentication, deployment, and operational workflows. I also learned that infrastructure changes must be reviewed for permissions, rollback, security, and user impact—not only for whether the deployment succeeds.
I still need to improve time estimation, concise explanation of architectural decisions, and deeper automated testing. These are the main areas I plan to continue developing after the internship.
Needs Improvement Continue improving problem-solving skills when deploying AWS services. Further develop technical presentation and communication skills. Broaden knowledge of cloud security, cost optimization, and system operations. Continue practicing observability, automated testing, and rollback design for deployment pipelines.

title: CI/CD and GitHub OIDC
content:
Scope GitHub Actions builds and tests the code. GitHub OIDC lets a workflow assume a temporary IAM role to upload artifacts, call SSM, and deploy without storing long-lived access keys.
Evidence to capture A successful Deploy frontend or backend workflow. The OIDC provider and trust policy with the account ID redacted. The IAM role and least-privilege permissions. GitHub repository variables by name only; never capture secret values.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
During the First Cloud AI Journey program, I had the opportunity to study AWS through a structured learning path, practice individual services, and record the results in a worklog. The program helped me connect theoretical knowledge with practical deployment tasks.
Overall evaluation Learning environment: The learning path is divided into weekly topics, making it easier to track progress and focus on each AWS subject. Mentor / team admin support: The guides, announcements, and communication channels provided useful direction when I faced difficulties during hands-on practice. Relevance to my major: The content is relevant to software development and cloud engineering, especially networking, servers, storage, databases, and containers. Learning and skill-development opportunities: I practiced reading technical documentation, configuring AWS services, verifying results, troubleshooting, and writing technical reports. Culture and teamwork: Sharing resources and discussing problems within the group created a supportive learning environment and allowed me to learn from other members’ experiences. Support for interns: The program provided a clear learning path, reference materials, and expected deliverables, which helped me organize my study time proactively. Most satisfying part What I liked most was the combination of theory and hands-on AWS practice. Completing each week made my progress visible, from creating an account and managing costs to deploying resources such as EC2, S3, RDS, and Lightsail.
Areas for improvement The program could add topic-based live Q&A sessions and checklists for common troubleshooting cases. This would help beginners identify the causes of configuration or permission issues more quickly.
Suggestions and wishes I hope the program continues updating its content with newer AWS services, adds more multi-service integration exercises, and provides opportunities to present the final work and receive practical feedback.
